title: Cap. VIII: Alien righteousness saves; alien guilt does not damn
pass_a_gloss: Suppose someone replies that believers are saved by a righteousness that is not theirs but Christ's, and so they could also be damned by an injustice that is not theirs. Chamier (via Placeus) says that person fails to see how unlike the two cases are. Damnation comes from justice; salvation comes from grace. If salvation itself ran on justice, another person's righteousness could not save us; and on the same footing another person's guilt could not damn us. Placeus closes: nothing more plain could have been wanted.
pass_b_english: But if someone objects that the faithful are saved on account of a righteousness not their own but Christ's, and that therefore they can also be damned on account of an alien injustice, he truly does not see that very different things are being compared. For damnation is from justice, but salvation is from grace. For if salvation itself were also from justice, an alien righteousness could not save us; so neither can an alien guilt damn. Nothing, I think, could have been wanted more expressly.
source_text: Quod si excipiat quis, servari fideles propter justitiam non suam, sed Christi: itaque posse etiam damnari, propter alienam injustitiam, is vero non videt comparari valde diversa. Nam damnatio est a justitia, salus autem a gratia. Nam si esset etiam ipsa a justitia, non posset nos aliena justitia servare: quare ne aliena quidem culpa damnare. Nihil, opinor, desiderari potuit disertius.
